It builds an **adjacency list**: an array `adj` of size \(N+1\). 
For each student \(i\) (`adj[i]`) holds a list of `Edge` objects, each containing a neighbour’s id (`node`) and a time value (`time`). 
When a friendship pair \((x,y)\) is read, two `Edge` objects are added: one to `adj[x]` pointing to \(y\) and one to `adj[y]` pointing to \(x\). 
The time stored in these edges is always `0` because the input does not provide any weights.

After building the graph, the program starts the spreading process from student 1. 
It creates a boolean array `visited` of size \(N+1\) and marks student 1 as visited. 
A queue of `Edge` objects is created. 
All neighbours of student 1 are put into the queue with a time of `1` (the moment they first learn the news) and are marked visited.

The main loop repeatedly removes the first element from the queue. 
For the removed element `curr`, the variable `time` is set to `curr.time`. 
Then every neighbour of `curr.node` is examined. 
If a neighbour has not been visited yet, it is marked visited and a new `Edge` containing that neighbour’s id and a time of `time + 1` is added to the back of the queue. 
Thus, nodes are processed in the order they are discovered: all nodes that learn the news at the same moment are processed before any node that learns it later.

The loop ends when the queue becomes empty. 
At that point, the variable `time` holds the moment when the last student was added to the queue, i.e., the moment when the last student learns the news. 
This value is printed as the result.

It builds an adjacency list: an array `adj` of size `NMAX` where each entry `adj[i]` is a list of `Edge` objects. 
Each `Edge` stores a neighbour node and a cost (the cost is always 1 in this problem). 
For every friendship line `x y` the program adds an `Edge(y,1)` to `adj[x]`. 
(Edges are not added in the opposite direction, but the input guarantees that the graph is undirected.)

After the graph is built, the program runs a routine that starts from node 1. 
It keeps three main structures:

* `visited[0…N]` – a boolean array that marks whether a node has already been taken out of the priority queue. 
* `d[0…N]` – an integer list that stores the current best known distance from node 1 to each node. 
 It is initialised with a very large value (`Integer.MAX_VALUE/2`) for all nodes except node 1, which gets 0. 
* `queue` – a priority queue that orders `Edge` objects by their `cost` field (the distance value). 
 Initially the queue contains a single entry `Edge(1,0)`.

The main loop repeatedly removes the entry with the smallest cost from the queue. 
Let that entry be `current`. 
The node `current.node` is marked as visited. 
If the cost stored in the entry is larger than the current best distance in `d`, the entry is ignored (this can happen because a better path was found earlier).

For every neighbour of `current.node` (obtained from `adj[current.node]`) the program checks whether that neighbour has already been visited. 
If not, it calculates a new possible distance `dist = d[current.node] + neigh.cost`. 
If this `dist` is smaller than the current value stored in `d[neigh.node]`, the program updates `d[neigh.node]` to `dist` and inserts a new `Edge(neigh.node, dist)` into the priority queue. 
Thus neighbours that can be reached more cheaply are queued for later processing.

The loop continues until the queue becomes empty.

It creates an array called `level` that can hold `students` vectors of integers. 
The vector `level[0]` is filled with the single value `1`, representing that student 1 knows the news at time 0.

For the current pair it scans all indices `i` from `0` to `students‑1`. 
At each index it checks whether exactly one of the two students of the pair is already stored in `level[i]`. 
If the first student (`parent`) is found in `level[i]` but the second (`child`) is not, the program puts `child` into the next vector `level[i+1]` and stops checking further indices for this pair. 
(If the second student were the one already present, the same test would add the first student to the next level, but the code only adds when the first student is present.)

After all pairs have been read, the program scans the `level` array from the beginning. 
It looks for the first index `i` whose vector is empty. 
When it finds such an index, it prints `i‑1` and stops. 
Thus the printed number is the highest index that contains at least one student, which corresponds to the last “time step” that received a new student.

It stores each friendship as a two‑element array inside a larger array called `matrix`. 
So `matrix[i][0]` and `matrix[i][1]` hold the two students that are friends in the i‑th pair.

An `ArrayList<Boolean>` called `elevi` is created with `n+1` positions (index 0 is unused). 
Each position represents whether a student already knows the news (`true`) or not (`false`). 
Initially all positions are set to `false`. 
The program then marks student 1 as knowing the news by setting `elevi[1]` to `true`. 
It also sets `elevi[0]` to `true` but this position is never used for a real student.

A counter `t` is used to count the number of time steps. 
The main loop continues until every entry in `elevi` is `true`. 
Inside the loop the following happens:

1. `t` is increased by one, representing the next time step. 
2. A temporary list `aux` is filled with all students that currently know the news. 
 This is done by scanning all indices from 1 to `n` and adding those whose `elevi` value is `true`. 
3. For each student stored in `aux`, the program scans every friendship pair in `matrix`. 
 If the current student is the first element of a pair, the second element of that pair is marked as knowing the news (`elevi[second] = true`). 
 If the current student is the second element, the first element is marked as knowing the news. 
 Thus every friend of the current student becomes informed during this time step.

After all students in `aux` have been processed, the loop repeats. 
At the start of the next iteration, the new set of informed students is collected again, and the process continues until no `false` values remain in `elevi`.

When the loop ends, the counter `t` holds the number of time steps that were needed for every student to know the news.

It builds a two‑dimensional array `a` of size `(n+1) × (m+1)` that acts as an adjacency matrix: `a[x][y]` is set to `1` when students `x` and `y` are friends. All other entries stay `0`. 

Two one‑dimensional arrays are also created: 
* `viz` – a visited flag for each student, initially `0` for all. 
* `ordine` – a level counter for each student, initially `-1` for all. 

The student with id 1 is the source of the news. The program sets `ordine[1] = 0` and marks that student as visited. 

The main processing loop runs `n` times. In each outer iteration it looks for all students whose `ordine` equals the current level `ordin` (starting with `0`). For every such student `j` it scans all possible neighbours `k` from `1` to `n`. If `a[j][k]` is `1` (meaning `j` and `k` are friends) and `viz[k]` is still `0` (meaning `k` has not yet heard the news), the program marks `k` as visited (`viz[k] = 1`) and assigns it the next level `ordine[k] = ordin + 1`. 

Thus, in each outer loop the program processes all students that learned the news in the previous time step, and gives their unvisited friends the next time step. The order of processing is by increasing level: first all level 0 students, then all level 1 students, and so on. 

After the loops finish, the program scans the `ordine` array to find the largest value, which represents the last time step at which any student learned the news. That maximum value is printed. 

In short, the program builds an adjacency matrix, then propagates a “time level” from student 1 to all others by repeatedly visiting all students at the current level and assigning the next level to their unvisited friends, finally outputting the greatest level reached.
